title: Sin Embargo and No Obstante: Setting Facts Against Each Other

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *sin embargo* and *no obstante* from B1 Unit 1, and *aunque* from A2 Unit 28. They set one fact against another: something is true, and yet something unexpected is also true. A dry valley full of life is a perfect example.

sections.title: Contrast connectors in the quebrada
rows: La quebrada es seca; sin embargo, muchas comunidades viven allí.
*sin embargo* + comma: a new clause that contrasts
El camino es largo; no obstante, la gente lo recorre desde hace siglos.
*no obstante* means the same, a bit more formal
Aunque la zona es seca, se cultivan maíz y papas.
*aunque* joins two clauses in one sentence
No hay mucha agua. Sin embargo, hay cultivos en los valles bajos.
after a full stop, *sin embargo* starts the new sentence

items.spanish: La quebrada es seca; sin embargo, muchas comunidades viven allí desde hace siglos.
items.english: The ravine is dry; however, many communities have lived there for centuries.

items.spanish: El camino es largo; no obstante, muchas caravanas lo recorrían.
items.english: The road is long; nevertheless, many caravans travelled it.

items.spanish: Aunque la zona es seca, se cultivan maíz y papas en los valles bajos.
items.english: Although the area is dry, corn and potatoes are grown in the lower valleys.

items.spanish: Hay poca agua. Sin embargo, hay cultivos en los valles bajos.
items.english: There is little water. However, there are crops in the lower valleys.

sections.content: *Sin embargo* and *no obstante* usually come after a full stop or a semicolon, with a comma after them. *Aunque* joins two clauses inside one sentence. Do not use *por eso* for contrast: it gives a result, not a contrast.
